channel_name: Invest Like the Best · Patrick O'Shaughnessy
video_title: How AI Is Repricing Every Software Company
gist: Vanta CEO Christina explains how a fast-growing, high-margin compliance SaaS company is navigating AI-driven multiple compression: eating token costs instead of marking them up, rebuilding the product around agents, competing in an inflated talent market, and expanding into security as AI-powered attackers chain low-severity flaws into critical exploits. She argues the market irrationally favors low-margin AI hypergrowth and that AI's high-excitement/low-trust era makes provable security more valuable.

insights.claim: Vanta's customers reject token-based pricing on AI agents: any markup on underlying model tokens invites a direct price/quality comparison against Claude, putting the application vendor in competition with the model labs.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of SaaS vendors whose AI monetization depends on marking up model tokens; that margin is structurally contestable.
insights.quote: if you're trying to mark up at all, users are very smart and you will lose on that comparison

insights.claim: Vanta is currently eating its LLM token costs rather than passing them through, accepting lower gross margin to maximize agent usage.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Expect gross-margin compression at AI-adopting SaaS incumbents during the 'usage/deployment phase'; monitor whether pricing catches up later.
insights.quote: We're eating the token cost right now.

insights.claim: About 25% of Vanta's customers use the autonomous agent workflow; the goal is 75%, on the belief that agent-driven usage materially improves net retention, with pricing to be sorted out later.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Agent adoption share is a leading indicator for NRR at AI-native SaaS; commercialization lags deployment.

insights.claim: Credit-based pricing schemes that obscure a token exchange rate are seen through by customers and don't solve the token-markup problem.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Credit-based AI pricing models (common across SaaS) may face customer pushback and churn risk.

insights.claim: Everyone wants outcome (really output) pricing, but defining the unit of work is hard: beyond clean cases like support tickets closed, units such as 'document drafted', 'alert closed', or 'account offboarded' multiply into dozens, creating cognitive overhead buyers don't want.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Outcome pricing works best where a single unambiguous unit exists (e.g. support); be cautious of vendors claiming outcome pricing in multi-task domains.

insights.claim: Security/compliance agents use far fewer tokens than coding agents; Christina ranks token intensity as coding first, then possibly legal/document drafting, with 'decision-action' workflows like Vanta's much lower, which lets Vanta optimize model choice for quality over cost.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Inference demand is concentrated in coding and drafting use cases; margin pressure from tokens varies sharply by vertical.

insights.claim: A fast-growing, high-margin software business like Vanta now trades at roughly a third to a quarter of the multiple it would have commanded four years ago, despite fundamentals being unchanged or better.
insights.speaker: Patrick O'Shaughnessy (host)
insights.so_what: Profitable high-growth SaaS is being de-rated by AI disruption fears; potential mispricing if the businesses keep compounding.

insights.claim: Christina argues an 80%-growth/80%-margin business should, over time, return more cash than a 160%-growth/30%-margin AI business, yet the market values the latter at 3-10x the multiple of the former, which she views as irrational.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Contrarian case for owning high-margin incumbent software against low-margin hypergrowth AI apps on a long horizon.

insights.claim: Many investors have become 'AI maximalists' willing to fund only the labs and physical-world AI (e.g. robotic tractors) with nothing in between, raising the cost of capital for traditional software companies.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Capital is concentrating at the extremes (labs, robotics); mid-layer SaaS faces harder financing and depressed private marks.

insights.claim: The host argues the cost of capital for software is rising because capital can be deployed at very high returns in AI for now, so investors demand agent-driven growth from legacy software.
insights.speaker: Patrick O'Shaughnessy (host)
insights.so_what: Opportunity cost of AI investments pressures SaaS multiples; watch for capital rotation if AI returns compress.

insights.claim: Bending Spoons has become the industry's 'grim reaper' meme: a buyer of software businesses in structurally disadvantaged markets; Christina says AI has made some once-attractive markets structurally bad so that even the best founder hits a brick wall ('market wins' over founder).
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Expect more PE/Bending Spoons-style take-privates of AI-disrupted SaaS; market structure matters more than management.

insights.claim: Christina observes old SaaS revenue/go-to-market tooling providers are running PE/Bending Spoons-style efficiency playbooks rather than building AI-native products, leaving room for startups attacking go-to-market technology.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Legacy rev-tech incumbents may be harvesting rather than reinvesting; AI-native GTM startups could take share.

insights.claim: Total compensation for Vanta's top people is roughly 10x what it was five years ago, and Christina believes it should be even higher and will keep accelerating.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Rising stock-based comp at private tech firms implies heavier dilution; a key cost line to watch as companies go public.
insights.quote: it's probably like a factor of 10.

insights.claim: The main counterforce to accelerating tech compensation would be renewed investor concern about dilution and stock-based comp, a debate active in 2022-23 but currently absent.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: If SBC scrutiny returns, high-comp AI-era companies could face valuation pressure; currently not priced in.

insights.claim: Pay bands have become meaningless in the AI talent war; compensation is set by competing offers, with rivals pitching candidates on rapid step-up valuations (e.g. join at $6B before a $10B round).
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Private AI valuation step-ups are being used as recruiting currency, which reinforces momentum in private marks.
insights.quote: comp bands are kind of a joke now

insights.claim: Secondary tender offers have become normalized and expected as part of compensation in startups; companies not running them must compensate employees in other ways.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Sustained demand for private secondary liquidity; tenders are now a recurring feature of late-stage private companies.

insights.claim: Christina says company/customer context is underhyped relative to functional skill: she would take a weaker salesperson who knows Vanta over a stronger generic one, and thinks AI labs building GTM teams overweight pure sales skill.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Institutional context is a durable moat for agents and people alike; favor companies that capture proprietary context.

insights.claim: Vanta credits its win in compliance automation to execution plus a 400-tool integration 'trust graph' (effectively a security data lake) that now powers its agents and lets it ship new products faster.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Proprietary integration data layers are what let incumbents defend against AI-native entrants.

insights.claim: Vanta says it serves about 16,000 customers globally with roughly five products, after starting eight years ago with SOC 2 compliance.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Scale of installed base is the platform for cross-selling security products.

insights.claim: Software defensibility has weakened: 'you're only as good as the last thing you shipped' because a competitor can vibe-code a product in a weekend, so continuous shipping is required.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Feature moats are eroding; favor software businesses with data/distribution moats over pure feature sets.

insights.claim: Vanta's product is now built around an agent that proposes and executes tasks (e.g. offboarding departed employees' accounts) with 'do this once / do this always' permissions and on-the-fly generated UI, replacing alert-only monitoring.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Shift from alerting to autonomous remediation is the template for incumbent SaaS repositioning.

insights.claim: Vanta generates charts on demand with its agent instead of embedding BI tools like Tableau, which Christina believes reflects what software will look like medium-to-long term.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Embedded BI/analytics vendors face substitution by agent-generated reporting.

insights.claim: Large, older codebases are much harder for coding agents; Vanta (following Notion, which was about nine months ahead) is modularizing its codebase so agents can fully understand smaller pieces, otherwise high-context engineers must babysit them.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Incumbents with legacy codebases capture less AI productivity uplift until they refactor; a hidden disadvantage vs startups.

insights.claim: Vanta's onboarding team kept building traditional SaaS wizards instead of an LLM approach because they believed they weren't allowed to fail; once leadership explicitly accepted the risk, they shipped a drag-in-messy-files LLM onboarding that works well.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Organizational risk tolerance, not talent, is often the blocker to AI adoption at incumbents.

insights.claim: Christina rates the degree to which AI changes how companies are built at 8-9 out of 10, while principles (people matter, everything is hard) stay the same.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals near-total operating-model change at software firms; laggards risk structural disadvantage.

insights.claim: A US enterprise prospect asked Vanta to switch off its AI features because a non-AI tool is much easier to get through procurement; Vanta refuses to build an off switch.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI procurement friction can slow diffusion and revenue recognition for AI-forward vendors.

insights.claim: The host argues diffusion risk is real (Christina agrees): an AI-native company can be 'right but early and therefore wrong' if enterprise adoption takes a decade.
insights.speaker: Patrick O'Shaughnessy (host)
insights.so_what: Time-horizon risk is underappreciated in AI bets; pace of enterprise adoption drives returns.

insights.claim: Christina calls post-training custom models overhyped: per inference providers, the real reason to post-train is cost, not quality, and much post-training is done for marketing to investors and customers.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Discount 'we trained our own model' claims in AI startup pitches as differentiation.
insights.quote: there is not a quality reason to do it there's like kind of a marketing reason to do it right now

insights.claim: Forward-deployed engineer (FDE) models are seen as unsustainable outside eight-figure contracts like Palantir's; applied to five- and six-figure contracts the economics are upside down, and FDE is essentially professional services rebranded.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: AI startups leaning on FDEs for small contracts may show weak unit economics once growth slows.

themes.theme: Security in the age of AI attackers

insights.claim: AI models are far more persistent than human attackers and increasingly chain many individually benign or low-severity issues into serious exploits, more so than finding novel zero-days.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Vulnerability prioritization tools face disruption; demand rises for machine-speed remediation.

insights.claim: Because AI turns low-severity findings into critical chains, security must move to fixing issues at machine speed as fast as they are found, making traditional prioritization obsolete; Christina expects a rocky transition.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Continuous pen-testing plus auto-patching agents is an emerging security category.

insights.claim: Vanta plans continuous pentest-and-remediate agents for cloud misconfigurations at AWS and Azure for smaller customers, targeting buyers who won't pay ~$150K for Wiz but could pay $40-50K, while conceding CrowdStrike will serve enterprises better.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Vanta is moving down-market into cloud security adjacent to Wiz; SMB/mid-market security pricing gap is the wedge.

insights.claim: CISOs are getting budget to overhaul enterprise risk programs by attaching requests to AI risk; Christina says the same request three years ago would have been deferred.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: AI-linked security and risk budgets are expanding; supportive for security/GRC vendors.

insights.claim: Governments at federal, state and local levels, in and outside the US, show heightened AI-driven FOMO for modernizing processes and software, a stated priority of the current US administration.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Public-sector modernization spending is a growing opportunity for software and security vendors.

insights.claim: Trust in software and tech companies is declining year over year (seen in data center and personal agent debates); Christina's thesis is AI has created high excitement but low trust, making provable, auditable security more valuable to customers, regulators and auditors.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for compliance/trust-verification platforms as proof-of-security requirements multiply.

insights.claim: Vanta frames its long-term path as a security platform stacking products on its existing data and agent, positioned as the marketplace connecting companies to enterprises, governments and regulators demanding proof of industrial-grade security.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Watch Vanta's expansion from compliance into security; potential IPO candidate targeting standalone scale.

insights.claim: Paris software companies are predominantly using Chinese open models, having switched after the US closed off Fable to non-Americans, due to business-continuity risk of depending on American models.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Geopolitical access risk is driving non-US adoption of Chinese open models; a headwind for US labs' international share.
insights.quote: We basically all switched to Chinese models when Trump uh closed Fable off to non-Americans

insights.claim: Christina sees the ecosystem around open-source model providers (deployment firms, tooling) as underbuilt relative to the big labs, despite consensus that open models will be very real.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Potential venture opportunity in tooling/services built on open-weight models.

insights.claim: Robotics is underweighted relative to software investing, despite rapidly improving models.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Robotics may offer better entry prices than crowded AI software.

insights.claim: Christina sees proportionally more new startups in cybersecurity and in go-to-market technology than in other areas.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Expect crowded early-stage competition in AI security and rev-tech.

insights.claim: Christina says the venture side is more echo-chambered and judged on short-term paper returns than companies, citing sentiment that firms not investing in a lab or inference provider in the last four years should shut down; she flags high entry prices for labs.
insights.speaker: Christina (Vanta CEO)
insights.so_what: Lab/inference valuations embed crowded consensus; entry price risk is high.
